title: Definitions of Statistics, Probability, and Key Terms

slides.title: Statistics
slides.body: Statistics is the collection, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of data.
slides.question: What data could help a college decide when to keep its library open?

slides.title: Descriptive statistics
slides.body: Descriptive statistics summarizes the data we observed.
slides.question: A survey finds that 36 of 60 students want later library hours. How could we summarize this result?

slides.title: Inferential statistics
slides.body: Inferential statistics uses sample evidence to draw conclusions about a population.
slides.question: Can those 60 responses tell us what all students want?

slides.title: Probability
slides.body: Probability measures how likely an event is.
slides.question: Does a 50% chance of heads guarantee five heads in ten tosses?

slides.title: Long-run probability
slides.body: A fair coin has probability 0.5 of heads on each independent toss.
slides.question: Why should 4,000 tosses usually give a proportion nearer 0.5 than four tosses?

slides.title: Population
slides.body: The population is the entire group a study concerns.
slides.question: To study this quarter's enrolled students, who belongs in the population?

slides.title: Sample
slides.body: A sample is the part of a population actually studied. Sampling is the process of selecting a sample.
slides.question: Would surveying one afternoon class give every student a chance to be included?

slides.title: Representative sample
slides.body: A representative sample reflects the characteristics of the population relevant to the study.
slides.question: Would a sample containing only morning classes represent all college students?

slides.title: Variable
slides.body: A variable is a characteristic recorded for each individual or object.
slides.question: For a library-hours survey, what could we record for each student?

slides.title: Numerical variables
slides.body: A numerical (quantitative) variable records an amount with meaningful numerical units.
slides.question: Is the number of library visits a numerical variable?

slides.title: Categorical variables
slides.body: A categorical (qualitative) variable assigns a label or category.
slides.question: Why is preferred study location categorical even if locations receive number codes?

slides.title: Classifying variables
slides.body: A survey records each student’s preferred study location and weekly library visits.
slides.question: Which variable is categorical, and which is numerical?

slides.title: Data
slides.body: Data are the observed values of a variable. One observed value is a datum.
slides.question: For the variable “number of library visits last week,” what could three data values look like?

slides.title: Parameter
slides.body: A parameter is a numerical summary of a population.
slides.question: What population percentage would the library-hours survey try to estimate?

slides.title: Statistic
slides.body: A statistic is a numerical summary of a sample.
slides.question: Of 60 surveyed students, 36 want later hours. What sample statistic can we calculate?

slides.title: Population or sample?
slides.body: A college enrolls 2,400 students. A researcher randomly selects 80 of them for a survey.
slides.question: Which group is the sample?

slides.title: Parameter or statistic?
slides.body: In a random sample of 80 students, 25% use the library on Fridays.
slides.question: Is 25% a parameter or a statistic?

slides.title: Variable or value?
slides.body: A survey asks each student how many courses they take. One response is 4.
slides.question: What is the variable, and what is the observed value?

slides.title: Mean
slides.body: The arithmetic mean, commonly called the average, is the sum of the values divided by their number.
slides.question: Five study rooms contain 2, 3, 3, 5, and 7 students. What is the mean occupancy?

slides.title: Proportion
slides.body: A proportion is a part divided by its corresponding whole.
slides.question: Of 40 reserved study rooms, 14 are unused. What proportion is unused?

slides.title: A question of scope
slides.body: A survey of 50 library visitors finds that 90% want longer library hours.
slides.question: How far beyond these 50 visitors would you trust that result?

slides.title: The terms in a mean study
slides.body: Synthetic study: estimate mean pages printed per student at a college. Randomly survey 60 students; observed counts include 8, 12, and 19.
slides.question: What are the population, sample, variable, data, parameter, and statistic?

slides.title: The terms in a proportion study
slides.body: Synthetic study: estimate the proportion of all campus printers needing repair. Inspect 20 randomly chosen printers; 3 need repair.
slides.question: What are the population, sample, variable, data, parameter, and statistic?

slides.title: Dot plots
slides.body: A dot plot places one dot per observation above a number line, stacking repeated values. Synthetic visits: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 4.
slides.question: How would a dot plot show where these observations cluster?

title: Data, Sampling, and Variation in Data and Sampling

slides.title: Qualitative data
slides.body: Qualitative data, also called categorical data, describe categories.
slides.question: Why is a course subject a category even if the school assigns it a number?

slides.title: Quantitative data
slides.body: Quantitative data, also called numerical data, record counts or measurements.
slides.question: Does the number 201 mean the same kind of thing in “room 201” and “201 seats”?

slides.title: Discrete data
slides.body: Quantitative discrete data take separated, countable values, commonly from counting.
slides.question: Can the number of open browser tabs be 4.5?

slides.title: Continuous data
slides.body: Quantitative continuous data measure quantities that can take any value within an interval.
slides.question: A download lasts 3.2 seconds. Could a more precise timer report 3.24 seconds?

slides.title: Continuous random variable
slides.body: A continuous random variable has possible numerical values throughout an interval.
slides.question: Could the unrounded time until a download completes be continuous?

slides.title: Classifying a variable
slides.body: A spreadsheet records each classroom's building name.
slides.question: What type of data is this?

slides.title: Classifying a count
slides.body: A spreadsheet records the number of chairs in each classroom.
slides.question: What type of data is this?

slides.title: Classifying a measurement
slides.body: A spreadsheet records each classroom's floor area in square meters.
slides.question: What type of data is this?

slides.title: Numbers as labels
slides.body: Students have identification numbers such as 10482 and 10517.
slides.question: Would the mean ID number describe a meaningful amount?

slides.title: Numbers recoded as categories
slides.body: A teacher records numerical quiz scores, then reports A, B, C, D, or F.
slides.question: How does converting scores to categories change the information retained?

slides.title: Bar graphs
slides.body: A bar graph compares category counts or percentages using bar lengths.
slides.question: For 12 blue, 8 black, and 5 red notebooks, what would the bars show?

slides.title: Pie charts
slides.body: A pie chart represents mutually exclusive parts of one whole.
slides.question: Among 25 notebooks, 12 are blue, 8 black, and 5 red. What fraction belongs to each slice?

slides.title: Pareto charts
slides.body: A Pareto chart orders category bars from largest to smallest.
slides.question: How would you arrange categories with counts 7, 19, 4, and 11?

slides.title: Overlapping categories
slides.body: Among 100 students, 65 use laptops and 55 use tablets. Some use both.
slides.question: Would these percentages make a valid two-slice pie chart?

slides.title: Missing responses
slides.body: A class has 30 students. A device survey records 18 laptops and 9 tablets, with one response per student.
slides.question: What is missing from this summary?

slides.title: Comparing different totals
slides.body: Synthetic surveys: Campus A has 40 tablet users among 100 respondents; Campus B has 60 among 200.
slides.question: Which campus has the larger proportion of tablet users?

slides.title: Simple random sampling
slides.body: Every possible sample of the chosen size has the same chance of selection.
slides.question: How could we choose 5 of 30 numbered students this way?

slides.title: Random sampling
slides.body: Random sampling uses chance to select population members. A simple random sample gives every group of the chosen size equal probability.
slides.question: Does selecting every tenth ID after a random start make every possible group equally likely?

slides.title: Random number selection
slides.body: Choose 4 different IDs from 01 through 20. Generated IDs: 07, 07, 23, 14, 02, 19.
slides.question: Which IDs enter the sample?

slides.title: Stratified sampling
slides.body: Divide the population into groups called strata. In proportional stratified sampling, randomly select the same fraction from every stratum.
slides.question: How could we sample 10% of students from each academic program?

slides.title: Cluster sampling
slides.body: Divide the population into groups called clusters. Randomly select clusters and include everyone in the selected groups.
slides.question: What sample results if we randomly choose three class sections and survey everyone in them?

slides.title: Systematic sampling
slides.body: After a random start, select every kth member of a list.
slides.question: On a list of 60 students, start at 4 and select every tenth student. Which IDs enter the sample?

slides.title: Convenience sampling
slides.body: A convenience sample uses readily available individuals.
slides.question: What could go wrong if a campus survey uses only students in the nearest classroom?

slides.title: Voluntary response
slides.body: A voluntary-response or self-selected sample consists of people who choose to respond to an open invitation.
slides.question: Who might respond to an online poll about parking fees?

slides.title: Strata or clusters?
slides.body: Plan A samples 5 students from every program. Plan B randomly chooses 2 programs and surveys everyone in them.
slides.question: Which plan uses clusters?

slides.title: Sampling with replacement
slides.body: Sampling with replacement returns a selected member before the next selection, allowing repeats.
slides.question: If a drawn numbered card is returned and shuffled in, can it appear again?

slides.title: Sampling without replacement
slides.body: Sampling without replacement allows each member to be selected only once.
slides.question: How does leaving each drawn card out change the next selection?

slides.title: Sampling variation
slides.body: Different random samples can produce different statistics.
slides.question: Two random samples report 42% and 47% support for a proposal. Must one be wrong?

slides.title: Sampling error
slides.body: Sampling error is the difference arising because a sample, rather than the whole population, is observed.
slides.question: Can an unbiased random sample still give a statistic different from the population parameter?

slides.title: Nonsampling error
slides.body: Nonsampling errors arise from problems such as inaccurate measurement, data entry, nonresponse, or biased design.
slides.question: Would recording 42 as 24 be sampling error or nonsampling error?

slides.title: Sample size and precision
slides.body: Larger random samples generally reduce sampling variability. They do not repair a biased selection procedure.
slides.question: Which helps more: enlarging a biased poll or correcting its selection method?

slides.title: Variation in data
slides.body: Observations within one sample can differ.
slides.question: Three printers take 9, 12, and 18 seconds for the same file. What might account for the variation?

slides.title: Sampling bias
slides.body: Sampling bias occurs when selection systematically favors some population members or outcomes.
slides.question: Would surveying 10,000 library visitors remove bias in a survey of all students?

slides.title: Nonresponse
slides.body: Nonresponse occurs when selected individuals do not provide data. A college randomly invites 400 students; only 35 reply.
slides.question: What concern remains even though the invitations were random?

slides.title: Question wording
slides.body: “Should the college waste money on longer library hours?”
slides.question: How could we ask about the same issue more neutrally?

slides.title: Undue influence
slides.body: Undue influence occurs when collection conditions or wording pressure people toward a response.
slides.question: How could asking about a service while its manager watches affect answers?

slides.title: Causality and confounding
slides.body: Association means variables vary together. Causality means one influences the other; confounding makes their effects difficult to separate.
slides.question: Do higher scores among voluntary tutoring users prove tutoring caused the difference?

slides.title: Self-funded studies
slides.body: A self-funded or self-interest study is supported by someone with a stake in its result.
slides.question: What methods and disclosures would you examine before accepting a software vendor’s study?

slides.title: A sampling choice
slides.body: A college wants feedback from both online and on-campus students.
slides.question: What sampling plan would you propose?

title: Frequency, Frequency Tables, and Levels of Measurement

slides.title: Frequency
slides.body: A frequency counts how often a value or category occurs.
slides.question: In 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, what is the frequency of 2?

slides.title: Frequency tables
slides.body: Number of downloads for 12 sessions:\n0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 0, 2, 1, 4, 2, 2
slides.question: What frequency table summarizes these data?

slides.title: Relative frequency
slides.body: Relative frequency = frequency / total number of observations.
slides.question: If 5 of 12 sessions have two downloads, what is their relative frequency?

slides.title: Percentages
slides.body: Seven of 20 printers are in use.
slides.question: What percentage of the printers is in use?

slides.title: Cumulative relative frequency
slides.body: Cumulative relative frequency adds relative frequencies through a value.
slides.question: If frequencies for 0, 1, 2, 3 downloads are 2, 3, 4, 1, what fraction have at most 2?

slides.title: Cumulative frequency
slides.body: Cumulative frequency counts observations at or below a cutoff. Synthetic frequencies for 0, 1, 2, 3 downloads: 2, 3, 4, 1.
slides.question: How many sessions have at most 2 downloads?

slides.title: At most or less than?
slides.question: What percentage have fewer than 2 downloads?

slides.title: More than a cutoff
slides.question: What percentage have more than 2 downloads?

slides.title: Checking a table
slides.body: A frequency table for 20 observations lists counts 4, 7, and 8.
slides.question: What should we check before interpreting it?

slides.title: Grouped data
slides.body: Download times in seconds: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 14
slides.question: How many times belong in each interval: 0 to less than 5, 5 to less than 10, 10 to less than 15?

slides.title: Reading a grouped frequency table
slides.body: Synthetic duration classes [0,5), [5,10), [10,15), [15,20) seconds have frequencies 2, 5, 8, 5.
slides.question: What percentage of durations are at least 5 but less than 15 seconds?

slides.title: Recovering interval frequency
slides.body: Synthetic cumulative relative frequencies at upper boundaries 5, 10, 15, 20 seconds are 0.10, 0.35, 0.75, 1.00.
slides.question: What relative frequency lies from 10 up to 15 seconds?

slides.title: Rounding
slides.body: Textbook convention: keep one more decimal place than the original data and round only the final result.
slides.question: For synthetic values 4, 5, and 8, what mean should we report?

slides.title: Rounding totals
slides.body: Three equally frequent categories each have relative frequency 1/3.
slides.question: Why might displayed percentages fail to total exactly 100%?

slides.title: Levels of measurement
slides.body: A level of measurement describes which comparisons are meaningful: category, order, differences, or ratios.
slides.question: Why should the measurement level affect which summaries we calculate?

slides.title: Nominal level
slides.body: The nominal scale has categories with no inherent order.
slides.question: What is the level of measurement for a printer's brand?

slides.title: Ordinal level
slides.body: The ordinal scale orders categories without defined numerical gaps.
slides.question: What can “poor, fair, good, excellent” tell us about service?

slides.title: Interval level
slides.body: The interval scale has meaningful numerical differences but no absolute zero representing none of the quantity.
slides.question: Does 20 degrees Celsius represent twice the temperature of 10 degrees Celsius?

slides.title: Ratio level
slides.body: The ratio scale has meaningful differences and ratios, with a zero representing none of the measured quantity.
slides.question: Does a 20-minute download take twice as long as a 10-minute download?

slides.title: Measurement level
slides.body: A tournament records first, second, and third place.
slides.question: What level of measurement is this?

slides.title: Measurement level
slides.body: A file list records sizes in bytes.
slides.question: What level of measurement is this?

slides.title: Choosing a summary
slides.body: A survey codes favorite browsers as 1, 2, 3, and 4.
slides.question: Would the mean of these codes answer a useful question?

slides.title: Observational studies
slides.body: An observational study records conditions without assigning treatments.
slides.question: Students choose whether to attend tutoring. We compare their exam scores. What kind of study is this?

slides.title: Experiments
slides.body: An experiment assigns treatments and measures outcomes. A randomized experiment uses chance to assign the treatments.
slides.question: A teacher randomly assigns two practice formats. What makes this an experiment?

slides.title: Experimental units
slides.body: An experimental unit is an individual or object that receives a treatment.
slides.question: Thirty printers are each assigned one of two paper types. What are the experimental units?

slides.title: Explanatory variables
slides.body: The explanatory variable, also called the independent variable, is the proposed influence on an outcome.
slides.question: A study compares two paper types for their effect on printer jams. What is the explanatory variable?

slides.title: Response variables
slides.body: The response variable, also called the dependent variable, is the measured outcome.
slides.question: How could we measure printer performance in the paper-type study?

slides.title: Treatments
slides.body: Treatments are the experimental conditions assigned to units.
slides.question: A printer study uses standard, recycled, and coated paper. What are the treatments?

slides.title: Lurking variables
slides.body: A lurking variable is an unaccounted-for influence on a study.
slides.question: Students who choose tutoring earn higher scores. What other influence might explain the difference?

slides.title: Confounding
slides.body: Confounding prevents us from separating the effects of different influences.
slides.question: One practice format is taught only by Teacher A, the other only by Teacher B. What is confounded?

slides.title: Random assignment
slides.body: Random assignment uses chance to allocate treatments.
slides.question: How could we assign 40 volunteers to two practice formats?

slides.title: Chance imbalance
slides.body: Forty volunteers are randomly assigned to two practice formats.
slides.question: Must the two groups begin with exactly equal prior knowledge?

slides.title: Random sampling or assignment?
slides.body: A researcher randomly selects 100 students, then lets each choose a practice format.
slides.question: Which part is random sampling, and is there random assignment?

slides.title: Control groups
slides.body: A control group provides a comparison condition.
slides.question: What would be a useful control group for a study of a new practice app?

slides.title: Placebos
slides.body: A placebo resembles a treatment but lacks its active component.
slides.question: Why might an inactive version of a treatment be useful in a comparison?

slides.title: Placebo effects
slides.body: A placebo effect is a response associated with expectations of treatment.
slides.question: How could a participant's expectations change a self-reported outcome?

slides.title: Blinding
slides.body: Blinding, also called masking, withholds treatment identities from specified people.
slides.question: Why might a grader receive assignments without knowing each student's practice group?

slides.title: Double blinding
slides.body: In a double-blind experiment, neither participants nor the people measuring outcomes know the treatment identities.
slides.question: Could students be blinded to whether their practice uses paper or an app?

slides.title: Replication
slides.body: Replication applies each treatment to multiple independent experimental units.
slides.question: Why would one printer per paper type be weak evidence?

slides.title: Causal conclusions
slides.body: Students who voluntarily use a new study app score higher than students who do not.
slides.question: Does this establish that the app caused the difference?

slides.title: A study design
slides.body: Forty volunteers will compare two versions of a practice app using the same final quiz.
slides.question: How would you design a fair experiment?

slides.title: When assignment is impossible
slides.body: A study compares performance across naturally occurring academic-year groups. Researchers cannot randomly assign a student’s year of study.
slides.question: How does this limit the study’s ability to establish causation?

slides.title: Treatment order
slides.body: Every volunteer tries two practice formats. Randomly choose which format each person uses first.
slides.question: Why might using the same format first for everyone confound the comparison?

slides.title: The parts of an experiment
slides.body: Synthetic study: randomly select 40 campus printers, assign standard or recycled paper, and count jams per 1,000 pages.
slides.question: What are the population, sample, experimental units, explanatory variable, response variable, and treatments?

slides.title: Participation and consent
slides.body: A researcher tells students that refusing a study will lower their course grades.
slides.question: What is ethically wrong with this recruitment?

slides.title: Informed consent
slides.body: Informed consent is voluntary agreement after understanding the study, its risks, costs, and potential benefits.
slides.question: What information should a participant receive before agreeing?

slides.title: Institutional Review Board
slides.body: An Institutional Review Board (IRB) reviews proposed human-subject research and protections for participants.
slides.question: Why should review occur before recruitment and data collection?

slides.title: Risk and benefit
slides.body: Ethical research minimizes risks and weighs them against anticipated benefits.
slides.question: How could a driving simulator reduce the risks of studying distraction?

slides.title: Privacy
slides.body: A public spreadsheet lists participant names beside individual quiz scores.
slides.question: How should these data be handled before sharing?

slides.title: Honest reporting
slides.body: A researcher deletes accurate low scores because they weaken the desired conclusion.
slides.question: What is wrong with this decision?

slides.title: Selective reporting
slides.body: A team runs ten comparisons and reports only the one with its preferred result.
slides.question: What information does the audience need to judge the evidence?

slides.title: Fabrication and falsification
slides.body: Fabrication invents observations. Falsification alters or selectively removes observations to misrepresent findings.
slides.question: What is wrong with copying completed survey responses to fill missing records?

slides.title: Stopping when results look favorable
slides.body: A team checks results repeatedly and stops as soon as the preferred conclusion appears.
slides.question: How could a prespecified data-collection plan improve the reliability of the study?

slides.title: Graph scales and ethical reporting
slides.body: Two graphs show the same synthetic rise from 98 to 102. One vertical axis starts at 0; the other starts at 97.
slides.question: How could the choice of scale influence a reader’s impression?

slides.title: Comparing complaint rates
slides.body: Synthetic service A has 30 complaints from 1,000 customers; B has 20 from 200.
slides.question: Would reporting only complaint counts give a fair comparison?

slides.title: A class data question
slides.body: Class activity: investigate the number of files students downloaded yesterday.
slides.question: What exactly should count as one download?

slides.title: Collecting observations
slides.body: Use anonymous IDs and record one download count per willing participant.
slides.question: What recording rules would make everyone's counts comparable?

slides.title: A systematic sample
slides.body: Practice roster: IDs 01-24. Select 8 IDs using a random start from 1, 2, or 3 and a step of 3.
slides.question: Which IDs does our random start select?

slides.title: A practice dataset
slides.body: Synthetic counts for 24 students, in ID order:\n0, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 5, 0, 1, 2, 6, 3,\n1, 4, 2, 0, 5, 3, 2, 1, 4, 2, 3, 6
slides.question: What are the download counts for our 8 selected IDs?

slides.title: An exact-value table
slides.body: Use our 8 selected download counts.
slides.question: What frequency table can we make for the values 0 through 6?

slides.title: Relative frequencies
slides.body: Use our exact-value table for the 8 sampled students.
slides.question: What are the relative frequencies?

slides.title: Cumulative frequencies
slides.body: Use our exact-value table for the 8 sampled students.
slides.question: What are the cumulative relative frequencies?

slides.title: A grouped table
slides.body: Regroup the same sample into 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, and 6 or more downloads.
slides.question: What relative frequency table results?

slides.title: Information lost in grouping
slides.body: Use our exact-value and grouped tables.
slides.question: Which table can determine the exact percentage with at most 2 downloads?

slides.title: Interpreting a cutoff
slides.body: Use our exact-value and grouped tables.
slides.question: Can both tables determine the exact percentage with at most 3 downloads?

slides.title: Above a cutoff
slides.body: Use the exact-value and grouped frequency tables from our download-count activity.
slides.question: Which table determines the exact percentage with more than 2 downloads?

slides.title: Above a class boundary
slides.body: Use the exact-value and grouped frequency tables from our download-count activity.
slides.question: Can both tables determine the percentage with more than 3 downloads?

slides.title: Choosing a grouping
slides.body: The same observations can be grouped as 0–1, 2–3, 4–5, 6+, or displayed separately.
slides.question: Is one table more correct, or do the tables answer different questions?

slides.title: A different starting point
slides.body: Repeat the systematic sample with a different starting ID.
slides.question: How does the percentage with at most 2 downloads change?

slides.title: Scope of the evidence
slides.body: A class collects real download counts only from its own willing participants.
slides.question: Which population could this sample reasonably describe?

slides.title: The sampling frame
slides.body:
Fictional campus printers:
North: N1, N2, N3, N4, N5, N6
South: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6
East: E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, E6
West: W1, W2, W3, W4, W5, W6
slides.question: How could we select printers to inspect?

slides.title: A simple random sample
slides.body: Use the 24-printer list from the first slide. Label the printers 01-24 in the displayed order.
slides.question: How can we randomly select 6 distinct printers so every group of 6 is equally likely?

slides.title: A systematic sample
slides.body: Use the same 24-printer list. Choose a random starting position from 1 through 4, then take every fourth printer.
slides.question: Which 6 printers enter our sample?

slides.title: Stratifying by building
slides.body: North, South, East, and West each contain 6 printers.
slides.question: How can we randomly select one-third of the printers in each building?

slides.title: A cluster sample
slides.body: Treat each of the four buildings as a cluster.
slides.question: How can we randomly select 2 buildings and inspect every printer in them?

slides.title: Same groups, different method
slides.body: Plan A selects 2 printers from each building. Plan B selects every printer in 2 randomly chosen buildings.
slides.question: How do the two selection procedures differ?

slides.title: Unequal strata
slides.body: A second campus has 12 printers in North, 8 in South, and 4 in East.
slides.question: For a proportional stratified sample of 6, how many should come from each building?

slides.title: Stratifying by another characteristic
slides.body: Fictional fleet: 16 black-and-white and 8 color printers. Select one-quarter of each type by simple random sampling.
slides.question: How many printers belong in each stratum’s sample?

slides.title: Rounding allocations
slides.body: Fictional strata contain 7, 9, and 12 printers. Select 25% from each and round each allocation to the nearest whole number.
slides.question: What sample sizes result, and does their sum equal exactly 25% of the fleet?

slides.title: Ordering matters
slides.body: A list repeats this sequence: color, black-and-white, black-and-white, black-and-white.
slides.question: What could happen if we sample every fourth printer?

slides.title: A reproducible procedure
slides.body: Another group must recreate our selection process using a fresh random draw.
slides.question: What details must our sampling description include?

slides.title: Choosing a method
slides.body: Travel between buildings is costly, but printers within one building may be very similar.
slides.question: Which sampling method would you choose, and what tradeoff would you accept?
